course.title: Data Structures & Algorithms
course.description: A hands-on introduction to the data structures and algorithms every programmer leans on — arrays, linked lists, hash tables, trees, and sorting — with running-time analysis throughout. Structure adapted from MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: Reading an element from an array by its index (e.g. a[7]) takes…
questions.explanation: Arrays store elements contiguously, so the address is computed directly — constant time. See 'Big-O analysis'.

questions.prompt: A stack removes elements in which order?
questions.explanation: A stack is LIFO — the most recently pushed item is popped first. See 'Key terms'.

questions.prompt: A queue removes elements in which order?
questions.explanation: A queue is FIFO — like a line at a shop. See 'Key terms'.

questions.prompt: The average-case cost of looking up a key in a hash table is…
questions.explanation: A good hash spreads keys evenly, giving expected constant-time lookup. See 'Hash tables'.

questions.prompt: An in-order traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys in…
questions.explanation: In-order (left, node, right) of a BST yields keys sorted ascending. See 'Trees & binary search trees'.

questions.prompt: Which sorting algorithm has an O(n log n) worst-case running time?
questions.explanation: Merge sort is O(n log n) in every case; the others listed are O(n^2) worst-case. See 'Sorting algorithms'.

questions.prompt: A breadth-first search (BFS) of a graph explores nodes using which structure?
questions.explanation: BFS uses a FIFO queue to visit nodes in order of increasing distance. See 'Key terms'.

questions.prompt: Two nested loops, each running over all n items, give a running time of…
questions.explanation: n iterations times n iterations is n^2 total work — quadratic. See 'Big-O analysis'.

lessons.title: Big-O: measuring how fast code grows
lessons.grammar_note: Big-O describes growth as input size n grows large — constants and lower-order terms drop out.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a piece of code and name its Big-O running time, and explain why constants don't matter. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what is the running time of two nested loops over n items?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text:
Big-O notation answers one question: as the input grows, how does the work grow? We count the *dominant* operation and ignore constant factors, because for large n a factor of 2 or 100 is dwarfed by the shape of the growth. O(1) is constant, O(log n) grows slowly, O(n) is linear, O(n log n) is 'linearithmic', and O(n^2) is quadratic. Here is a linear-time function that checks for a duplicate using a set:
```python
def has_duplicate(nums):
    seen = set()
    for x in nums:
        if x in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(x)
    return False
```
Each element is visited once and each set operation is expected O(1), so the whole function is O(n).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Let's trace `has_duplicate([3, 1, 3, 7])` step by step. Start with `seen = set()`. x=3: not in seen, add it → seen={3}. x=1: not in seen, add it → seen={1, 3}. x=3: it *is* in seen → return True immediately (the last two elements are never examined).
```python
print(has_duplicate([3, 1, 3, 7]))
```
Output:
```python
True
```
Contrast this with the naive approach of comparing every pair with two nested loops: that would be O(n^2). The set-based version trades a little memory for a big speed-up.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Name the Big-O of each: (1) reading a[0] from a list; (2) a single loop from 0 to n-1; (3) two nested loops each from 0 to n-1; (4) halving the search range each step until one item remains; (5) has_duplicate above. Answers: (1) O(1); (2) O(n); (3) O(n^2); (4) O(log n); (5) O(n).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: keeping constants, e.g. writing O(2n) — drop the 2, it's O(n). Mistake: adding when you should nest — a loop *inside* a loop multiplies, giving O(n^2), not O(2n). Exit: (a) Is O(500) the same class as O(1)? (b) A loop that doubles a counter until it exceeds n runs how many times? Answers: yes, both are constant time; about log2(n) times, so O(log n).

lessons.title: Arrays and linked lists
lessons.grammar_note: Arrays give O(1) indexing but O(n) insertion at the front; linked lists flip that trade-off.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain the trade-offs between arrays and linked lists and traverse a singly linked list in code. Warm-up: what is the cost of reading a[7] from an array?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text:
An *array* (Python's list) stores elements in one contiguous block, so indexing is O(1) — but inserting at the front means shifting every later element, which is O(n). A *linked list* stores each value in a node that points to the next node. Prepending a new node is O(1) because nothing shifts, but there is no direct indexing: to reach the k-th value you must follow k pointers, which is O(n). Here is a singly linked list:
```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, nxt=None):
        self.value = value
        self.nxt = nxt

def to_list(head):
    out = []
    node = head
    while node is not None:
        out.append(node.value)
        node = node.nxt
    return out
```

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Let's build the chain 10 → 20 → 30 and walk it. `Node(30)` has nxt=None; `Node(20, Node(30))` points to it; `Node(10, ...)` is the head. `to_list` starts at head, appends 10, moves to the 20 node, appends 20, moves to the 30 node, appends 30, then node becomes None and the loop stops.
```python
head = Node(10, Node(20, Node(30)))
print(to_list(head))
```
Output:
```python
[10, 20, 30]
```
Notice we never used an index — we only followed `nxt` pointers, one hop at a time.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Give the Big-O for each operation: (1) array indexing a[k]; (2) inserting at the front of an array; (3) prepending a node to a linked list; (4) finding the k-th value in a linked list; (5) appending to the end of a linked list when you already hold a tail pointer. Answers: (1) O(1); (2) O(n); (3) O(1); (4) O(n); (5) O(1).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming linked lists are always faster — random access is O(n), so arrays win when you index a lot. Mistake: forgetting the `node = node.nxt` step, which loops forever. Exit: (a) Which structure gives O(1) indexing? (b) Which gives O(1) prepend? Answers: the array; the linked list.

lessons.title: Hash tables
lessons.grammar_note: Hash tables give expected O(1) lookup; collisions can degrade the worst case to O(n).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how a hash table achieves fast lookup and use a dictionary to count items. Warm-up: what is the average-case cost of a hash-table lookup?

sections.heading: The idea
Worked example
sections.text:
Trace `word_count(["a", "b", "a", "c", "a"])`. Start counts={}. 'a': get returns 0 → counts={'a': 1}. 'b': get returns 0 → counts={'a': 1, 'b': 1}. 'a': get returns 1 → counts={'a': 2, 'b': 1}. 'c': get returns 0 → counts={'a': 2, 'b': 1, 'c': 1}. 'a': get returns 2 → counts={'a': 3, 'b': 1, 'c': 1}.
```python
print(word_count(["a", "b", "a", "c", "a"]))
```
Output:
```python
{'a': 3, 'b': 1, 'c': 1}
```
Python 3.7+ dicts keep insertion order, so 'a', 'b', 'c' print in the order they were first seen.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) average-case lookup cost? (2) worst-case lookup cost with many collisions? (3) what does counts.get(w, 0) return when w is absent? (4) do dict keys have to be sorted for O(1) lookup? (5) is a hash table a good choice for 'is this value present?' queries? Answers: (1) O(1); (2) O(n); (3) 0; (4) no; (5) yes — expected O(1) membership tests.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: expecting hash tables to keep keys in sorted order — they don't; use a tree for that. Mistake: assuming O(1) is guaranteed rather than expected. Exit: (a) What is a collision? (b) Which structure would you pick for fast membership tests, a hash table or a linked list? Answers: two keys mapping to the same slot; the hash table.

questions.prompt: Prepending a node to a singly linked list is…
questions.explanation: No elements shift — you just point the new node at the old head.

questions.prompt: Reading the k-th element of a singly linked list is…
questions.explanation: You must follow k pointers from the head — linear in the worst case.

questions.prompt: The set-based has_duplicate function runs in…
questions.explanation: One pass over the list with expected O(1) set operations.

questions.prompt: A hash-table lookup when almost every key collides into one slot is…
questions.explanation: All colliding keys must be scanned — the worst case is linear.

questions.prompt: In counts.get(w, 0), what is returned if w is not a key yet?
questions.explanation: The second argument is the default returned when the key is missing.

questions.prompt: Inserting at the front of a Python list (array) is…
questions.explanation: Every existing element must shift one slot to the right.

lessons.title: Trees and binary search trees
lessons.grammar_note: A balanced BST gives O(log n) search; a degenerate one degrades to O(n). In-order traversal yields sorted keys.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Insert keys into a binary search tree and read them back in sorted order. Warm-up: in what order does an in-order traversal of a BST visit the keys?

sections.heading: The idea
Worked example
sections.text:
Insert 5, 3, 8, 1, 4 in that order. 5 becomes the root. 3 < 5 → left child of 5. 8 ≥ 5 → right child of 5. 1 < 5 → go left to 3; 1 < 3 → left child of 3. 4 < 5 → go left to 3; 4 ≥ 3 → right child of 3. The tree is: 5 at the root; left subtree rooted at 3 with children 1 and 4; right child 8. An in-order traversal visits 1, 3, 4, then 5, then 8.
```python
root = None
for key in [5, 3, 8, 1, 4]:
    root = insert(root, key)
print(inorder(root))
```
Output:
```python
[1, 3, 4, 5, 8]
```
The output is sorted even though we inserted the keys out of order — that is the defining property of a BST's in-order walk.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) search cost in a balanced BST? (2) search cost in a degenerate (chain-like) BST? (3) what order does in-order traversal produce? (4) after inserting 6 into the tree above, is it a left or right child of 8? (5) which subtree of any node holds the smaller keys? Answers: (1) O(log n); (2) O(n); (3) sorted ascending; (4) left child of 8 (since 6 ≥ 5 goes right to 8, then 6 < 8 goes left); (5) the left subtree.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming a BST is always O(log n) — only if it stays balanced. Mistake: confusing in-order with pre-order; only in-order gives sorted output. Exit: (a) What keeps BST search fast? (b) Which traversal prints keys in sorted order? Answers: staying balanced so each step halves the keys; in-order traversal.

lessons.title: Sorting algorithms
lessons.grammar_note: Insertion sort is O(n^2) worst-case but O(n) on already-sorted input; merge sort is O(n log n) in every case.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Trace insertion sort by hand and compare it with merge sort's running time. Warm-up: which of the two, insertion sort or merge sort, has an O(n log n) worst case?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text:
*Insertion sort* builds a sorted region one element at a time: it takes the next element and slides it left past everything larger. It is O(n^2) in the worst case (reverse-sorted input) but only O(n) when the input is already sorted, because nothing slides. *Merge sort* instead splits the list in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges them; it is O(n log n) in *every* case, which is why large datasets favor it. Here is insertion sort:
```python
def insertion_sort(a):
    a = a[:]
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key = a[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = key
    return a
```

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Trace `insertion_sort([5, 2, 4, 1])`. i=1, key=2: a[0]=5 > 2, shift 5 right, place 2 → [2, 5, 4, 1]. i=2, key=4: a[1]=5 > 4, shift 5 right; a[0]=2 is not > 4, place 4 → [2, 4, 5, 1]. i=3, key=1: a[2]=5 > 1 shift; a[1]=4 > 1 shift; a[0]=2 > 1 shift; place 1 at front → [1, 2, 4, 5].
```python
print(insertion_sort([5, 2, 4, 1]))
```
Output:
```python
[1, 2, 4, 5]
```
The last element (1) had to travel all the way to the front, which is exactly the kind of work that makes insertion sort quadratic when the input is badly ordered.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) insertion sort's worst-case running time? (2) insertion sort's running time on already-sorted input? (3) merge sort's worst-case running time? (4) does insertion sort here modify the caller's original list? (5) which algorithm would you pick to sort a million random numbers? Answers: (1) O(n^2); (2) O(n); (3) O(n log n); (4) no — `a = a[:]` copies it first; (5) merge sort, for its O(n log n) guarantee.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: claiming insertion sort is always slow — it is excellent (O(n)) on nearly-sorted data. Mistake: expecting merge sort to sort in place with no extra memory — the standard version needs O(n) auxiliary space. Exit: (a) When is insertion sort O(n)? (b) What is merge sort's worst-case time? Answers: when the input is already (or nearly) sorted; O(n log n).

questions.prompt: An in-order traversal of a binary search tree returns the keys…
questions.explanation: Left, node, right visits smaller keys first — sorted ascending.

questions.prompt: Search in a balanced binary search tree is…
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the remaining keys.

questions.prompt: A BST built from already-sorted input degrades search to…
questions.explanation: The tree becomes a chain, so search walks it linearly.

questions.prompt: Insertion sort's worst-case running time is…
questions.explanation: Reverse-sorted input forces every element to slide fully left.

questions.prompt: Insertion sort on an already-sorted list runs in…
questions.explanation: Nothing slides, so it makes a single linear pass.

questions.prompt: Merge sort's worst-case running time is…
questions.explanation: It splits in half (log n levels) and merges n elements per level.

lessons.title: Applied project: choose the right structure

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Design a small program that reads a stream of words and reports the three most frequent ones. You will not submit running code — you'll plan it rigorously, choosing data structures and justifying their running times.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State which structure you'd use to count word frequencies, and its expected per-word cost. 2) Explain how you'd extract the top three counts, and the cost of that step. 3) Give the overall Big-O of your design in terms of the number of words n. 4) Name one input that would make your chosen structure perform worse than expected, and why.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ You chose a hash table (dict) for counting and stated expected O(1) per word. ✔ Your top-three step is described concretely (e.g. one linear scan tracking three maxima, or sorting the counts). ✔ Your overall running time is justified, not just asserted — counting is O(n), a linear top-three scan keeps the whole design O(n). ✔ You named a realistic worst case (e.g. adversarial keys all colliding into one hash slot, degrading lookups toward O(n)). If all four hold, you're reasoning like an algorithms engineer.
